sections.body_md:
A descent method is an iteration with three separate decisions. At the current point, compute the gradient. From that gradient, build a direction whose directional derivative is negative. Then choose a positive step length, and replace the point by the point plus the step length times the direction. After the update, apply a stopping test. A small gradient norm is the usual test, because a vanishing gradient means the first-order model has nowhere useful to go.

The direction is where the methods differ. Steepest descent takes the negative gradient. A scaled method takes \(-D \nabla f\) with a positive definite \(D\), which stretches the coordinates before the step. Newton's method takes \(-H^{-1} \nabla f\) when the Hessian is positive definite, so the direction solves the quadratic model exactly. Gauss-Newton is the least-squares relative of that idea: it linearizes the residual and solves a linear least-squares subproblem, which inverts a Gram matrix of the residual Jacobian rather than the full Hessian of the objective.

The step length is an independent choice. It may be a fixed number, the exact minimizer of the objective along the line, or the result of a backtracking loop. Stopping is independent again. None of these choices changes the shape of the update. They only fill in the direction, the length, and the decision to halt.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The update, a steepest direction, and a Newton direction are
\[
x^+ = x + t d, \qquad d = -\nabla f(x), \qquad d = -H_f(x)^{-1} \nabla f(x).
\]
The step length satisfies \(t > 0\), and \(d\) is a descent direction.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Start at \((8, 1)\) with direction \((-1, 2)\) and step length \(1\). The new point is \((8, 1) + (-1, 2) = (7, 3)\).

The crate coordinate is 7. The squared length of the displacement is \(1 + 4 = 5\), which is \(t^2\) times the squared length of the direction. Whether this direction was steepest, scaled, or Newton is a separate question. The update rule does not ask. It only adds the accepted step. A stopping test would then look at the gradient at \((7, 3)\), not at the old point.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Adding the gradient instead of its negative is the sign error that turns the iteration into ascent. The framework asks for a descent direction, and the gradient itself has a positive directional derivative whenever it is nonzero. A second miss is to treat the step length as part of the direction. Scaling \(d\) by two and then using \(t = 1\) is the same ray as the original \(d\) with \(t = 2\), so the two decisions have to be stated together. A third is to stop because a direction was found. Finding a direction is the start of the iteration, not evidence that the gradient is small. A fourth is to invert the Hessian when it is indefinite and still call the result a descent direction. Negative curvature can make \(-\nabla f^T H^{-1} \nabla f\) positive.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: On a positive definite quadratic the step along a fixed direction has a closed form. A sufficient-decrease test accepts a trial that falls enough without finding that exact minimizer. Gauss-Newton sits in the same loop as one more way to build \(d\), from a linearized residual.
